1eiflvd:239: Amazon Q's decision to evaluate ACLs at query time rather than index time carries deeper implications: it transforms permission control from a data engineering problem into a runtime decision problem. Index-time evaluation requires knowing "who will access what" at data ingestion time, which complicates the indexing pipeline in multi-tenant or dynamic permission scenarios. Query-time evaluation allows the index to remain unchanged, with permission decisions made only when the user makes a request. This means the same S3 bucket can serve users across different permission domains without maintaining a separate index for each permission combination. However, this also means ACL misconfigurations are discovered at runtime rather than being caught at data ingestion time.

gd30zs:288: Fail-closed behavior (deny-by-default) is not just a technical feature—it represents a philosophical shift in access control for enterprise AI systems. In traditional RBAC, administrators are accustomed to a "default-allow, explicit-deny" mindset. In document-level ACL scenarios, the automatic denial of unlisted resources means zero fault tolerance in permission management: any ACL configuration omission directly causes some users to "not see" documents they should have access to. This zero-default-tolerance model is necessary in highly regulated scenarios like HR and finance, but it also imposes higher demands on ACL maintenance processes—every newly added prefix and user must have explicit ALLOW rules, otherwise it will generate a flood of "can't see the document" tickets in daily operations.
